rules.title: The cramfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The cramfs filesystem is a compressed, read-only filesystem intended for systems with limited memory. A cramfs image can be mounted and used without first decompressing the image.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling cramfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The freevxfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The freevxfs filesystem is a free implementation of the Veritas filesystem and is the primary filesystem type used on HP-UX systems.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling freevxfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The hfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfs file system type is a hierarchical file system that allows Mac OS file systems to be mounted.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling hfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The hfsplus kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfsplus filesystem type is a hierarchical filesystem designed to replace hfs and allowing Mac OS filesystems to be mounted.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling hfsplus when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The jffs2 kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The jffs2 file system type (Journalling Flash File System 2) is a log-structured file system used on flash memory devices.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling jffs2 when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The squashfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The squashfs filesystem is a compressed, read-only filesystem often used for LiveCD and similar images. A squashfs image can be mounted without first decompressing it.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling squashfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The udf kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The udf file system type is the Universal Disk Format used to implement the ISO/IEC 13346 and ECMA-167 specifications. It is an open-vendor file system type for storing data on a wide range of media. This file system type is required to support DVD writing and newer optical disc formats.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the system's local attack surface. If this filesystem type is not needed, disable it.

rules.title: The usb-storage kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The usb-storage kernel module enables the system to use USB mass-storage devices such as flash drives and external disks.
rules.impact: Restricting USB access on the system will reduce the physical attack surface of the device and reduce possible malware introduction vectors.
rules.scope: See section 1.1.1.8 in CentOS Linux 7 v4.0.0 (Audit/Remediation).

rules.title: /tmp is a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /tmp directory is a world-writable directory used for temporary storage by all users and some applications. IF an entry for /tmp exists in /etc/fstab, it takes precedence over entries in the default systemd unit file. Note: In an environment where the primary system is diskless and attached via iSCSI, entries in /etc/fstab may not take precedence. /tmp can be configured to use tmpfs. tmpfs places everything in the kernel's internal caches, grows and shrinks to accommodate the files it contains, and can swap unnecessary pages out to swap space. It has maximum-size limits that can be adjusted on the fly with the mount -o remount command. Because tmpfs resides entirely in the page cache and swap, all tmpfs pages are shown as "Shmem" in /proc/meminfo and "Shared" in free. Note that these counters also include shared memory. The most reliable way to obtain a count is to use df and du. tmpfs has three mount options to define size: • size: the limit of allocated bytes for this tmpfs instance. The default is half of physical RAM without swap. If you exceed the size of tmpfs instances, the machine will lock up because the OOM handler will be unable to free that memory. • nr_blocks: Same as size, but in PAGE_SIZE blocks. • nr_inodes: the maximum number of inodes for this instance. The default is half the number of pages of physical memory, or (on a highmem machine) the number of lowmem RAM pages, whichever is smaller. These parameters accept a k, m, or g suffix and can be changed on remount. The size parameter also accepts a % suffix to limit this tmpfs instance to that percentage of physical RAM. By default, if neither size nor nr_blocks is specified, size=50% is used.
rules.impact: Creating a dedicated file system for /tmp allows the administrator to set additional mount options, such as the noexec option, which makes /tmp useless for an attacker installing executable code. It will also prevent an attacker from creating a hard link to a system setuid program and waiting for it to be updated. After the program is updated, the hard link would be broken and the attacker would have their own copy of the program. If a security vulnerability were discovered in the program, the attacker could continue to exploit the known vulnerability. This can be done either by mounting tmpfs on /tmp or by creating a separate partition for /tmp.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option to ensure that users cannot create block or character special devices in /tmp.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp filesystem is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /tmp.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option indicates that the file system cannot contain executable binaries.
rules.impact: Because the /tmp file system is intended only for temporary file storage, set this option to ensure that users cannot execute binaries from /tmp.

rules.title: /dev/shm is a separate partition
rules.explanation: The /dev/shm directory is world-writable and can function as shared memory facilitating inter-process communication (IPC).
rules.impact: Creating /dev/shm as its own file system allows the administrator to set additional mount options, such as the noexec option, which makes /dev/shm useless to an attacker for installing executable code. It will also prevent an attacker from creating a hard link to a setuid system program and waiting for it to be updated. After the program is updated, the hard link will be broken and the attacker will have their own copy of the program. If a security vulnerability were found in the program, the attacker could continue to exploit the known vulnerability. This can be done by mounting tmpfs on /dev/shm.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nodev on /dev/shm prevents creation of device nodes in shared memory that could bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /dev/shm prevents setuid binaries from being executed from shared memory for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /dev/shm reduces the risk that shared memory will be used as an in-memory execution staging area for malicious code.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /home
rules.explanation: The /home directory is used to satisfy local users' disk space needs.
rules.impact: By default, only a single / partition is created. Because the /home directory contains user-generated data, there is a risk of resource exhaustion. Essentially, the entire disk is available to be filled, affecting the system as a whole. In addition, other operations on the system may fill the disk independently of /home and affect all local users. Configuring /home as its own file system allows the administrator to set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev. These options limit an attacker's ability to create exploits on the system. For /home, options such as usrquota/grpquota can be considered to limit the impact users can have on each other with respect to disk resource exhaustion. Other options allow specific behavior. See man mount for exact details of file-system-independent and file-system-specific options. Because /home contains user data, care should be taken to protect the security and integrity of the data and the mount point.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /home
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because the /home filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option to ensure that users cannot create block or character special devices in /home.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /home
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because the /home filesystem is intended only for storing user files, set this option to ensure that users cannot create setuid files in /home.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var
rules.explanation: The /var directory is used by daemons and other system services for temporary storage of dynamic data. Some directories created by these processes may be world-writable.
rules.impact: The rationale for placing /var on a separate partition is as follows. A default installation creates only a single / partition. Because the /var directory can contain world-writable files and directories, there is a risk of resource exhaustion. In effect, the entire disk would be available to fill and thereby impact the system as a whole. In addition, other operations on the system can fill a disk unrelated to /var and cause unexpected system-wide behavior because the disk is full. See man Auditd.conf for details. Configuring /var as a separate filesystem allows the administrator to set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev. These options limit the ability of attackers to create exploits on the system. Other options enable specific behavior. See man mount for precise details on filesystem-independent and filesystem-dependent options. An example of /var being used would be an attacker creating a hard link to a setuid system program and waiting for it to be updated. After the program is updated, the hard link would be broken and the attacker would retain their own copy of the program. If a security vulnerability were discovered in the program, the attacker could continue to exploit the known vulnerability.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because the /var filesystem is not intended to support devices, set this option to ensure that users cannot create block or character special devices in /var.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because the /var file system is intended only for variable files such as logs, set this option so that users cannot create setuid files in /var.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/tmp
rules.explanation: /var/tmp provides temporary storage that persists across reboots. Placing it on a separate partition enables restrictive mount options while isolating that storage from the root filesystem.
rules.impact: Isolating /var/tmp limits persistence of attacker-controlled temporary files across reboots and allows protective mount options on this writable location.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nodev on /var/tmp prevents creation of device nodes in persistent temporary storage that could bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /var/tmp prevents setuid binaries from persisting across reboots in temporary storage for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /var/tmp reduces the risk that persistent temporary storage will be used to stage and execute malicious binaries across reboots.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log
rules.explanation: The /var/log directory is used by system services to store log data.
rules.impact: A default installation creates only one / partition. Because the /var/log directory contains log files that can become quite large, there is a risk of resource exhaustion. In effect, it would have the entire disk available to fill and affect the system as a whole. Configuring /var/log as a separate file system allows the administrator to set additional mount options such as noexec/nosuid/nodev. These options limit the ability of attackers to create exploits on the system. Other options allow specific behavior. See man mount for exact details of file-system-independent and file-system-specific options. Because /var/log contains log files, care should be taken with the security and integrity of the data and the mount point.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nodev on /var/log prevents creation of device nodes in the log directory that could bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /var/log prevents setuid binaries from being executed from the log directory if write access is obtained.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /var/log ensures the log partition remains storage-only and reduces the risk of executing binaries planted in log directories.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The /var/log/audit directory stores audit daemon logs. Placing it on a separate partition isolates audit storage from other log growth and supports compliance retention.
rules.impact: Isolating /var/log/audit helps preserve audit records when other logs grow rapidly and reduces the chance that audit capacity will be exhausted by unrelated logging.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nodev on /var/log/audit prevents creation of device nodes in audit log storage that could bypass device-access controls.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /var/log/audit prevents setuid binaries from being executed from the audit log partition.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /var/log/audit keeps the audit partition storage-only and reduces the risk of executing binaries planted among audit logs.

rules.title: GPG keys are configured
rules.explanation: Most package managers implement GPG key signing to verify package integrity during installation.
rules.impact: It is important to ensure that updates are obtained from a valid source to protect against spoofing that could result in unintentional installation of malware on the system.

rules.title: Package manager repositories are configured
rules.explanation: Package metadata and packages are installed only from repositories whose signatures are verified. Unsigned or third-party repositories let anyone who controls the mirror decide what is installed as root.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Updates, patches, and additional security software are installed
rules.explanation: The package provides controls the rest of the baseline depends on; it must be installed and kept current through the distribution repositories.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: AppArmor is installed
rules.explanation: AppArmor provides mandatory access control.
rules.impact: Without a mandatory access control system installed, only the default discretionary access control system will be available.

rules.title: AppArmor is enabled in the bootloader configuration
rules.explanation: AppArmor is enabled for early boot by passing kernel parameters such as apparmor=1 and security=apparmor through the bootloader configuration.
rules.impact: If AppArmor is not enabled at boot, confinement profiles are not applied during system startup, leaving processes unprotected until AppArmor is activated later.

rules.title: All AppArmor profiles are in enforce or complain mode
rules.explanation: Loaded AppArmor profiles should be active in either enforce mode (policy violations are blocked) or complain mode (violations are logged). Profiles that are unloaded or unconfined provide no confinement.
rules.impact: Inactive or unconfined profiles leave applications without MAC restrictions, increasing the impact of a compromised process.

rules.title: All AppArmor profiles are enforcing
rules.explanation: AppArmor profiles define which resources applications may access.
rules.impact: Security configuration requirements vary from site to site. Some sites may require a more restrictive policy than the default, which is acceptable. This item is intended to ensure that any policies present on the system are enabled.

rules.title: A bootloader password is set
rules.explanation: Setting a bootloader password will require anyone who reboots the system to enter a password before they can set boot parameters from the command line.
rules.impact: Requiring a boot password when the bootloader runs prevents an unauthorized user from entering boot parameters or modifying the boot partition. This prevents users from weakening security (for example, disabling AppArmor at boot).
rules.scope: Parameters net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra in /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/*

rules.title: Bootloader configuration access is configured
rules.explanation: Ensure that bootloader configuration access is configured.
rules.impact: Setting permissions to read and write for the root user only prevents non-root users from viewing or modifying boot parameters. Non-root users who read boot parameters may identify security weaknesses at boot time and exploit them.

rules.title: Address space layout randomization is enabled
rules.explanation: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) randomizes the locations of key process memory regions such as the stack, heap, and shared libraries. A value of 2 enables full randomization.
rules.impact: Randomizing virtual memory region placement makes memory-page exploits harder to write because memory layout continually changes.

rules.title: Ptrace_scope is restricted
rules.explanation: The ptrace system call provides a means by which one process (the "tracer") can observe and control the execution of another process (the "tracee"), and also inspect and modify the memory and registers of the traced object.
rules.impact: If a single application is compromised, an attacker will be able to attach to other running processes (for example, Bash, Firefox, SSH sessions, the GPG agent, and so on) to obtain additional credentials and continue expanding the scope of the attack. Enabling restricted mode will limit a compromised process's ability to use PTRACE_ATTACH on other processes running under the same user. In restricted mode, ptrace will continue to work for the root user.

rules.title: Core dumps are restricted
rules.explanation: A core dump is the memory of an executable program. It is typically used to determine why a program crashed. It can also be used to obtain sensitive information from the core file. The system provides the ability to set a soft limit for core dumps, but a user can bypass it.
rules.impact: Setting a hard limit on core dumps prevents users from overriding the soft limit. If core dumps are required, consider setting limits for user groups (see limits.conf(5)). In addition, setting the fs.suid_dumpable variable to 0 will prevent setuid programs from dumping core.

rules.title: Prelink is not installed
rules.explanation: prelink is a program that modifies ELF shared libraries and dynamically linked ELF binaries so that the time required for the dynamic linker to perform relocations at startup is significantly reduced.
rules.impact: The prelink feature can interfere with AIDE because it modifies binary files. Prelinking can also increase system vulnerability if an attacker is able to compromise a shared library such as libc.

rules.title: Automatic error reporting is not enabled
rules.explanation: Ensure that automatic error reporting is not enabled.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: The message of the day is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The /etc/motd file displays a message after successful login. It should present an authorized-use notice and avoid disclosing detailed system or kernel version information.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: The local login warning banner is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue file is displayed before local login. It should contain an authorized-access warning and avoid technical details about the system.
rules.impact: System details in the local login banner provide reconnaissance information before authentication and can weaken the clarity of authorized-use notices.

rules.title: The remote login warning banner is configured correctly
rules.explanation: The /etc/issue.net file is displayed to remote users before login (for example via SSH). It should contain an authorized-access warning without disclosing OS type or version.
rules.impact: Remote banner disclosure of OS details assists reconnaissance before authentication and can undermine the legal and policy value of an authorized-use notice.

rules.title: Access to /etc/motd is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/motd are displayed to users after login and act as a message of the day for authenticated users.
rules.impact: - IF - /etc/motd is not configured with correct access, it can be modified by unauthorized users using incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Access to /etc/issue is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before they log on at local terminals.
rules.impact: - IF - the /etc/issue file is not configured with correct access, it may be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Access to /etc/issue.net is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before login for remote connections from configured services.
rules.impact: - IF - the /etc/issue.net file is not configured with correct access, it may be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: GDM is removed
rules.explanation: GNOME Display Manager (GDM) is a program that manages graphical display servers and handles graphical user login.
rules.impact: If a graphical user interface (GUI) is not required, it should be removed to reduce the system attack surface.

rules.title: The GDM login banner is configured
rules.explanation: GDM is the GNOME display manager that provides graphical logon for GNOME-based systems.
rules.impact: Warning banners inform users who attempt to log on of their legal status with respect to the system and should include the name of the organization that owns the system and any existing monitoring policies.

rules.title: The GDM disable-user-list option is enabled
rules.explanation: GDM is the GNOME Display Manager, which provides graphical logon for GNOME-based systems. The disable-user-list setting controls whether the user list is displayed on the logon screen.
rules.impact: Displaying a user list eliminates half of the username-and-password equation that an unauthorized person would need to log on to the system.

rules.title: GDM screen lock when the user is idle
rules.explanation: Ensure GDM screen lock when the user is idle
rules.impact: If /etc/motd does not have the correct owner, it may be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: GDM screen lock cannot be overridden
rules.explanation: Ensure that GDM screen lock cannot be overridden.
rules.impact: If /etc/issue does not have the correct owner, it may be modified by unauthorized users with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: GDM automounting of removable media is disabled
rules.explanation: The setting is turned off so that the feature it enables cannot be used against the host.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: GDM automatic mounting of removable media is not overridden
rules.explanation: Ensure that GDM automatic mounting of removable media is not overridden.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: GDM autorun is never enabled
rules.explanation: The autorun-never parameter allows the GNOME Display Manager to disable autorun via GDM.
rules.impact: Malware on removable media can exploit AutoRun features when the media is inserted into the system and launched.

rules.title: GDM autorun-never is not overridden
rules.explanation: The autorun-never setting allows the GNOME desktop display manager to disable autorun via GDM. Using lock mode in dconf, you can prevent users from changing certain settings. To lock a dconf key or subpath, create a locks subdirectory in the key-file directory. Files in this directory contain a list of keys or subpaths to lock. As with key files, you can add any number of files to this directory.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: XDMCP is not enabled
rules.explanation: The X Display Manager Control Protocol (XDMCP) is intended to provide authenticated access to display manager services for remote displays.
rules.impact: XDMCP is inherently insecure. • XDMCP is not an encrypted protocol. This may allow an attacker to intercept keystrokes entered by the user. • XDMCP is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. This may allow an attacker to steal legitimate users' credentials by impersonating the XDMCP server.

rules.title: Autofs services are not in use
rules.explanation: autofs automatically mounts devices, typically including CD/DVD and USB drives.
rules.impact: If automounting is enabled, anyone with physical access can attach a USB drive or disk and access its contents in the filesystem, even if they do not have permission to mount it themselves.

rules.title: Avahi-daemon services are not in use
rules.explanation: Avahi is a free zeroconf implementation that includes a multicast DNS/DNS-SD service discovery system. Avahi allows programs to publish and discover services and hosts running on a local network without special configuration. For example, a user can connect a computer to the network and Avahi automatically finds printers to print to, files to browse, people to communicate with, and network services running on the computer.
rules.impact: Automatic discovery of network services is generally not required for system operation. It is recommended to remove this package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: DHCP server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) is a service that allows machines to be assigned IP addresses dynamically. There are two versions of the DHCP protocol: DHCPv4 and DHCPv6. At startup the server can be started for one or the other using the -4 or -6 arguments.
rules.impact: Unless the system is specifically configured to operate as a DHCP server, it is recommended to remove this package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: DNS server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Domain Name System (DNS) is a hierarchical naming system that maps names to IP addresses of computers, services, and other resources connected to the network.
rules.impact: Unless the system is specifically intended to operate as a DNS server, it is recommended to remove the package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Dnsmasq services are not in use
rules.explanation: dnsmasq is a lightweight tool that provides DNS caching, DNS forwarding, and DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) services.
rules.impact: Unless the system is specifically intended as a DNS cache, DNS forwarder, and/or DHCP server, it is recommended to remove the package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: FTP server services are not in use
rules.explanation: File Transfer Protocol (FTP) provides networked computers with the ability to transfer files.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Ldap server services are not in use
rules.explanation: An LDAP server (such as slapd) provides directory services for authentication and organizational data.
rules.impact: If the system will not need to operate as an LDAP server, it is recommended to remove the software to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Message access server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Message access servers such as IMAP and POP3 (for example Dovecot) provide remote access to stored email mailboxes.
rules.impact: These services may contain vulnerabilities and provide an entry point for attackers. If they are not used, they should be disabled to reduce the attack surface.

rules.title: Network file system services are not in use
rules.explanation: The component is not required on this host. Removing it eliminates the parser, protocol implementation or daemon it would otherwise expose.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: NIS server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Network Information Service (NIS) (formerly known as "Yellow Pages") is a client-server directory service protocol for distributing system configuration files. The NIS server is a set of programs that allow configuration files to be distributed. The NIS client (ypbind) was used to bind a computer to an NIS server and obtain distributed configuration files.
rules.impact: ypserv.service is inherently an insecure system that is vulnerable to DoS attacks, buffer overflows, and poor authentication for NIS map queries. NIS has generally been replaced by protocols such as Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). It is recommended that ypserv.service be removed and that other, more secure services be used.

rules.title: Print server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Common Unix Printing System (CUPS) provides the ability to print to both local and network printers. A system running CUPS can also accept print jobs from remote systems and print them on local printers. It also provides the ability to administer the service remotely via the web.
rules.impact: If the system is not required to print jobs or accept print jobs from other systems, it is recommended to remove CUPS to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Rpcbind services are not in use
rules.explanation: The rpcbind utility maps RPC services to the ports they listen on. RPC processes notify rpcbind at startup, registering the ports they listen on and the RPC program numbers they intend to serve. A client system then contacts rpcbind on the server with a specific RPC program number. rpcbind.service redirects the client to the correct port number so it can contact the requested service. Portmapper is an RPC service that always listens on TCP and UDP 111 and is used to map other RPC services (such as nfs, nlockmgr, quotad, mountd, and so on) to the corresponding port number on the server. When a remote host makes an RPC call to this server, it first consults the port map to determine where the RPC server is listening.
rules.impact: A small request (~82 bytes over UDP) sent to Portmapper generates a large response (amplification from 7x to 28x), making it a suitable tool for DDoS attacks. If rpcbind is not required, it is recommended to remove the rpcbind package to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Rsync services are not in use
rules.explanation: The rsync service can be used to synchronize files between systems over network channels.
rules.impact: rsync.service poses a security risk because the rsync protocol is unencrypted. The rsync package should be removed to reduce the system's attack surface.

rules.title: Samba file server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Samba implements SMB/CIFS file and print sharing for interoperability with Windows and other SMB clients.
rules.impact: If SMB file sharing is not required, removing Samba reduces a substantial network attack surface commonly used for lateral movement.

rules.title: Snmp services are not used
rules.explanation: Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) is a widely used protocol for monitoring the status and health of network equipment, computer hardware, and devices such as UPS units. Net-SNMP is a suite of applications used to implement SNMPv1 (RFC 1157), SNMPv2 (RFC 1901–1908), and SNMPv3 (RFC 3411–3418) over both IPv4 and IPv6. Support for classic SNMPv2 (also known as "historic SNMPv2" — RFC 1441–1452) was discontinued in version 4.0 of the UCD-snmp package. The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) server is used to listen for SNMP commands from an SNMP management system, execute commands or collect information, and then send the results back to the requesting system.
rules.impact: An SNMP server can communicate using SNMPv1, which transmits data in cleartext and does not require authentication to execute commands. SNMPv3 replaces the simple/cleartext password exchange used in SNMPv2 with more securely encoded parameters. If the SNMP service is not required, the snmpd package should be removed to reduce the system attack surface. Note: If SNMP is required: • The server should be configured for SNMP v3 only. User authentication and message encryption must be configured. • If SNMP v2 is absolutely necessary, change the community string values.

rules.title: TFTP server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) is a simple protocol for exchanging files between two TCP/IP computers. TFTP servers allow a TFTP client to connect to send and receive files.
rules.impact: If there is no need to run the system as a TFTP server, it is recommended that the package be removed to reduce the potential attack surface. TFTP has no built-in encryption, access control, or authentication. This allows an attacker to easily use TFTP to gain access to files.

rules.title: Web proxy server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Web servers such as Apache and Nginx serve HTTP/HTTPS content. Hosts that are not designated web servers should not run these services.
rules.impact: Unnecessary web servers expand the network attack surface and may expose internal content or web application vulnerabilities.

rules.title: Web server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Web servers provide the ability to host website content.
rules.impact: If running a web server service on the system is not approved at the local site, web server packages should be removed to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Xinetd services are not in use
rules.explanation: The X Window System provides a graphical user interface (GUI) in which users can have multiple windows to run programs and various add-ons. The X Window System is typically used on workstations where users log on, but not on servers where users typically do not log on.
rules.impact: If your organization does not specifically require graphical login access via X Windows, remove it to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: X Window Server services are not in use
rules.explanation: An X Window System server provides graphical display services. Production servers typically do not require a local graphical environment.
rules.impact: On servers, a graphical interface is generally not required and increases the attack surface, consumes resources, and may contain vulnerabilities.

rules.title: The mail transfer agent is configured for local-only mode
rules.explanation: A mail transfer agent (MTA) such as Postfix relays and delivers email. Binding the MTA to localhost restricts it to local delivery rather than accepting network mail.
rules.impact: An MTA listening on external interfaces can be abused as an open relay and exposes mail-protocol attack surface on hosts that should only send local mail.

rules.title: Only approved services listen on the network interface
rules.explanation: Ensure that only approved services listen on the network interface.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: The NIS client is not installed
rules.explanation: Network Information Service (NIS), formerly known as "Yellow Pages," is a client-server directory service protocol used to distribute system configuration files. The NIS client was used to bind a machine to an NIS server and obtain the distributed configuration files.
rules.impact: The NIS service is inherently an insecure system that is vulnerable to DoS attacks and buffer overflows and has weak authentication for NIS map queries. NIS has typically been replaced by protocols such as Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). It is recommended that the service be removed.

rules.title: The rsh client is not installed
rules.explanation: The rsh-client package contains client commands for rsh services.
rules.impact: These legacy clients contain numerous security threats and have been replaced by the more secure SSH package. Even if the server is removed, it is best to ensure that the clients are also removed so that users cannot accidentally attempt to use these commands and thereby expose their credentials. Note that removing the rsh-client package removes the clients for rsh, rcp, and rlogin.

rules.title: The talk client is not installed
rules.explanation: Talk software allows users to send and receive messages between systems through a terminal session. The talk client, which allows talk sessions to be initiated, is installed by default.
rules.impact: The software poses a security threat because it uses unencrypted protocols for communication.

rules.title: The telnet client is not installed
rules.explanation: The telnet package contains the telnet client, which allows users to establish connections to other systems using the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: The telnet protocol is insecure and unencrypted. Using an unencrypted transmission medium may allow an unauthorized user to steal credentials. The ssh package provides an encrypted session and increased security and is included in most Linux distributions.

rules.title: The ldap client is not installed
rules.explanation: LDAP client utilities (such as ldap-utils) query directory services. Hosts that do not need to query LDAP typically do not require these tools.
rules.impact: If the system will not need to act as an LDAP client, it is recommended to remove the software to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The FTP client is not installed
rules.explanation: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is a traditional and widely used standard tool for transferring files between a server and clients over a network, especially where authentication is not required (allowing anonymous users to connect to the server).
rules.impact: Presence of an FTP client increases the risk of cleartext credential exposure during file transfer. SFTP or other encrypted methods are preferred.

rules.title: A single time synchronization daemon is in use
rules.explanation: Accurate system time is required for authentication protocols, certificate validation, and reliable log timestamps. Exactly one NTP/time-synchronization daemon should provide timekeeping.
rules.impact: Conflicting or absent time synchronization can break Kerberos and TLS validation and undermine forensic correlation of log events across systems.

rules.title: An authorized time server is configured in systemd-timesyncd
rules.explanation: Ensure that an authorized time server is configured in systemd-timesyncd.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Systemd-timesyncd is enabled and running
rules.explanation: When systemd-timesyncd is the selected time-synchronization client, it should be enabled at boot and actively running.
rules.impact: Correct time synchronization is critical to system security, including the accuracy of timestamps in logs and the functioning of time-based authentication mechanisms.

rules.title: An authorized time server is configured in Chrony
rules.explanation: The cramfs filesystem type is a compressed, read-only Linux filesystem embedded in small systems. A cramfs image can be used without prior decompression of the image.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Chrony runs as the _chrony user
rules.explanation: Chrony can drop privileges and run as the unprivileged _chrony user rather than remaining root for routine operation.
rules.impact: Running chronyd with least privilege limits the impact of a compromise of the time-synchronization daemon.

rules.title: Chrony is enabled and running
rules.explanation: chrony is a daemon for synchronizing the system clock over the network.
rules.impact: chrony must be enabled and running to synchronize the system with a time server. Time synchronization is important to support time-sensitive security mechanisms and to ensure consistency of timestamps in log files across the enterprise, which aids forensic investigations.

rules.title: The cron daemon is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The cron daemon is used to run batch jobs on the system.
rules.impact: Although the system may not have user jobs that need to run, the system has maintenance jobs that may include security monitoring that must run, and cron is used to execute them.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/crontab are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/crontab file defines system-wide cron schedules. Restrictive ownership and mode limit who can read or modify those jobs.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/crontab can introduce jobs that run with elevated privileges, providing persistence or privilege abuse.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.hourly are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.hourly directory contains scripts executed hourly by cron, typically with root privileges.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/cron.hourly can place scripts that run hourly as root, enabling persistence and privilege abuse.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.daily are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.daily directory contains scripts executed daily by cron, typically with root privileges.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/cron.daily can place scripts that run daily as root, enabling persistence and privilege abuse.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.weekly are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.weekly directory contains scripts executed weekly by cron, typically with root privileges.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/cron.weekly can place infrequently run root jobs that are harder to notice during routine monitoring.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.monthly are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.monthly directory contains scripts executed monthly by cron, typically with root privileges.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/cron.monthly can place infrequently run root jobs that provide long-lived persistence.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/cron.d are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.d directory holds drop-in cron schedule files processed by the cron daemon.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/cron.d can introduce named cron jobs that execute with elevated privileges on an attacker-chosen schedule.

rules.title: Crontab is restricted to authorized users
rules.explanation: Access to user crontab can be controlled with /etc/cron.allow (allowlist) or /etc/cron.deny. An allowlist model restricts crontab use to explicitly authorized users.
rules.impact: Unrestricted crontab access allows any local user to schedule recurring jobs, increasing the impact of account compromise and complicating monitoring.

rules.title: At is restricted to authorized users
rules.explanation: The at command allows fairly complex time specifications, extending the POSIX.2 standard. It accepts time in HH:MM format to run a job at a specified time of day. (If that time has already passed, the next day is assumed.) You can also specify midnight, noon, or teatime (4:00 p.m.), and append an "AM" or "PM" suffix to the time of day to run in the morning or evening. You can also specify the day on which the job will run by giving a date in month-name day format with an optional year, or by specifying a date in MMDD[CC]YY, MM/DD/[CC]YY, DD.MM.[CC]YY, or [CC]YY-MM-DD format. The date specification must follow the time-of-day specification. You can also specify a time such as "now" + count time-units, where the time units may be minutes, hours, days, or weeks, and you can specify that the job run today by adding the suffix "today" to the time, and run the job tomorrow by adding the suffix "tomorrow" to the time. The files /etc/at.allow and /etc/at.deny determine which users may submit commands for later execution via at or batch. The file format is a list of usernames, one per line. Spaces are not allowed. If /etc/at.allow exists, only the usernames listed in it are permitted to use at. If /etc/at.allow does not exist, /etc/at.deny is checked, and every username not mentioned in it is permitted to use at. An empty /etc/at.deny file means that every user may use at. If neither file exists, only the superuser may use at.
rules.impact: On many systems, only the system administrator is authorized to schedule jobs. Using the at.allow file to control who can run jobs enforces this policy. It is easier to manage an allow list than a deny list. On a deny list, you could potentially add a user ID to the system and forget to add it to the deny files.

rules.title: The IPv6 status is defined
rules.explanation: Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) is the most recent version of the Internet Protocol (IP). It is designed to provide IP addressing and additional security to support the expected growth in connected devices. IPv6 is based on 128-bit addressing and can support 340 undecillion, that is 340 trillion cubed, addresses. IPv6 features: • Hierarchical addressing and routing infrastructure • Stateful and stateless configuration • Quality of Service (QoS) support • An ideal protocol for neighboring node interaction
rules.impact: IETF RFC 4038 recommends developing applications with dual stack in mind. It is recommended to enable IPv6 and configure it according to the recommendations. -IF- dual stack and IPv6 are not used in your environment, IPv6 can be disabled to reduce the system's attack surface, and recommendations specific to IPv6 can be skipped. Note: It is recommended to enable and configure IPv6 unless this conflicts with local site policy.

rules.title: Wireless interfaces are disabled
rules.explanation: Wireless networking is used when wired networks are unavailable.
rules.impact: IF wireless is not used, wireless devices can be disabled to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: Bluetooth services are not in use
rules.explanation: Bluetooth is a short-range wireless technology standard used to exchange data between devices over short distances. It uses UHF radio waves in the ISM bands from 2.402 GHz to 2.48 GHz. It is primarily used as an alternative to wired connections.
rules.impact: An attacker may find a way to access or damage your data. One example of this kind of activity is bluesnarfing, which refers to attackers using a Bluetooth connection to steal information from your Bluetooth device. In addition, viruses or other malicious code may use Bluetooth technology to infect other devices. If you are infected, your data may be damaged, compromised, stolen, or lost.

rules.title: The dccp kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) is a transport-layer protocol that supports multimedia streaming and telephony. DCCP provides the ability to obtain congestion control without implementing it at the application layer, but it does not provide in-order delivery.
rules.impact: IF the protocol is not required, it is recommended not to install the drivers in order to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The sctp kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) is a transport-layer protocol that supports message-oriented communication with multiple streams in a single association.
rules.impact: Setting the flag to 0 ensures that a multi-interface system can never forward packets and therefore will never serve as a router.

rules.title: The rds kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The Reliable Datagram Sockets (RDS) protocol is a transport-layer protocol designed to provide low-latency, high-throughput communication between cluster nodes. It was developed by Oracle Corporation.
rules.impact: -IF- the protocol is not used, it is recommended not to load the kernel module by disabling the service to reduce the potential attack surface.

rules.title: The tipc kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: TIPC (Transparent Inter-Process Communication) is a protocol used by some clustered applications for inter-node messaging.
rules.impact: Unnecessary protocol support increases the local attack surface. Disabling TIPC when cluster software does not require it reduces that exposure.

rules.title: IP forwarding is disabled
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.ip_forward and net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding flags are used to tell the system whether it may forward packets.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.ip_forward and net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding to 0 ensures that a system with multiple interfaces (for example, a hard proxy) can never forward packets and therefore will never function as a router.

rules.title: Packet redirect sending is disabled
rules.explanation: ICMP redirects are used to send routing information to other hosts. Because the host itself does not act as a router (in a host-only configuration), there is no need to send redirects.
rules.impact: An attacker can use a compromised host to send invalid ICMP redirects to other router devices in an attempt to disrupt routing and provide users access to a system configured by the attacker rather than a valid system.

rules.title: Bogus ICMP responses are ignored
rules.explanation: Setting net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses to 1 prevents the kernel from logging bogus responses (not conforming to RFC-1122) from broadcast frames, preventing filesystems from being filled with useless log messages.
rules.impact: Some routers (and some attackers) send responses that violate RFC-1122 and attempt to fill the log file system with large numbers of useless error messages.

rules.title: ICMP broadcast requests are ignored
rules.explanation: Setting net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts to 1 will cause the system to ignore all ICMP echo requests and timestamps to broadcast and multicast addresses.
rules.impact: Accepting ICMP echo requests and timestamps with broadcast or multicast destinations for your network can be used to cause your host to start (or participate in) a Smurf attack. A Smurf attack is based on an attacker sending a large number of ICMP broadcast messages with a spoofed source address. All hosts that receive this message and respond will send echo replies back to the spoofed address, which is likely not routable. If many hosts respond to the packets, the volume of traffic on the network can increase significantly.

rules.title: ICMP redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: ICMP redirect messages are packets that convey routing information and instruct your host (acting as a router) to send packets along an alternate path. This mechanism allows an external routing device to update your system's routing tables.
rules.impact: ICMP redirect messages are packets that convey routing information and tell your host (acting as a router) to send packets along an alternate path. This is a way to allow an external routing device to update your system's routing tables. By setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects, net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects, net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects, and net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects to 0, the system will not accept any ICMP redirect messages and therefore will not allow outsiders to update the system's routing tables.

rules.title: Secure ICMP redirects are not accepted
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are similar to ICMP redirects, except they originate from gateways listed in the default gateway list. These gateways are assumed to be known to your system and are most likely safe.
rules.impact: Even known gateways can still be compromised. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects and net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects to 0 protects the system from routing table updates from possibly compromised known gateways.

rules.title: Reverse path filtering is enabled
rules.explanation: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter and net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter to 1 forces the Linux kernel to use reverse path filtering for a received packet to determine whether the packet is valid. Essentially, with reverse path filtering, if the return packet does not leave from the same interface from which the corresponding original packet arrived, the packet is dropped (and logged if log_martians is set).
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter and net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter to 1 is a good way to prevent attackers from sending your system spoofed packets that cannot be answered. One case where this feature does not work is when asymmetric routing is used. This can occur when using dynamic routing protocols (bgp, ospf, and so on) on your system. If you use asymmetric routing on your system, you will not be able to enable this feature without breaking routing.

rules.title: Source-routed packets are not accepted
rules.explanation: Ensure that source-routed packets are not accepted.
rules.impact: Attackers use SYN attacks for denial of service; the targeted system receives many SYN packets without completing the three-way handshake. This quickly consumes slots in the kernel's half-open connection queue and prevents legitimate connections. SYN cookies allow the system to accept valid connections even while it is under a denial-of-service attack.

rules.title: Logging of suspicious packets
rules.explanation: If this feature is enabled, packets with non-routable source addresses are logged in the kernel log.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians and net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians to 1 enables this feature. Logging these packets allows the administrator to investigate the possibility that an attacker is sending spoofed packets to the system.

rules.title: TCP SYN cookies are enabled
rules.explanation: If tcp_syncookies is set, the kernel will process TCP SYN packets normally until the half-open connection queue fills, after which SYN cookie functionality takes effect. SYN cookies work by not using the SYN queue at all. Instead, the kernel simply replies to the SYN with a SYN|ACK, but includes a specially crafted TCP sequence number that encodes the source and destination IP addresses, port number, and the time the packet was sent. A legitimate connection will send the ACK packet of the three-way handshake with the specially crafted sequence number. This allows the system to verify that it received a valid response to the SYN cookie and to allow the connection even if there is no corresponding SYN in the queue.
rules.impact: Attackers use SYN flood attacks to deny service to the targeted system by sending many SYN packets without completing the three-way handshake. This rapidly consumes slots in the kernel's half-open connection queue and prevents successful connections. Setting net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies to 1 enables SYN cookies, allowing the system to continue accepting valid connections even when a denial-of-service attack is occurring.

rules.title: IPv6 router advertisements are not accepted
rules.explanation: IPv6 Router Advertisements (RA) advertise default routers and prefixes used for address autoconfiguration on a link.
rules.impact: Accepting unsolicited RAs can allow attackers to inject rogue IPv6 routers and redirect traffic, including on hosts primarily using IPv4.

rules.title: UFW is installed
rules.explanation: Uncomplicated Firewall (ufw) is an interface to iptables that is particularly well suited to host-based firewalls. ufw provides a framework for managing Netfilter as well as a command-line interface for managing the firewall.
rules.impact: A firewall utility is required to configure the Linux kernel Netfilter framework via the iptables or nftables backend. A host-based firewall based on the Linux kernel Netfilter can protect against threats originating from the corporate network, including malicious mobile code and poorly configured software on the host. Note: Only one firewall utility should be installed and configured. UFW depends on the iptables package.

rules.title: Iptables-persistent is not installed together with ufw
rules.explanation: iptables-persistent and UFW both manage persistence of iptables-based rules. Installing both can cause conflicting restore behavior at boot.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: The ufw service is enabled
rules.explanation: Uncomplicated Firewall (ufw) is a frontend for iptables. ufw provides a framework for managing Netfilter, as well as a command-line and graphical user interface for managing the firewall. Note: • When running ufw enable or starting ufw through its init script, ufw will flush its chains. This is necessary so that ufw can maintain a consistent state, but it may break existing connections (for example, SSH). ufw supports adding rules before enabling the firewall. • Before running ufw enable, execute the following command. # ufw allow proto tcp from any to any port 22 • Rules will still be reset, but the SSH port will be open after the firewall is enabled. Note that once ufw is "enabled", ufw will not flush chains when adding or removing rules (but it will when changing a rule or the default policy). • By default, ufw will prompt when enabling the firewall while working over SSH. This can be disabled using ufw --force enable.
rules.impact: The ufw service must be enabled and running so that ufw can protect the system.

rules.title: UFW loopback traffic is configured
rules.explanation: Configure the loopback interface to accept traffic. Configure all other interfaces to deny traffic to the loopback network (127.0.0.0/8 for IPv4 and ::1/128 for IPv6).
rules.impact: Loopback traffic is generated between processes on the computer and is typically critical to system operation. The loopback interface is the only place where loopback network traffic should be seen (127.0.0.0/8 for IPv4 and ::1/128 for IPv6). All other interfaces should ignore traffic on this network as an anti-spoofing measure.

rules.title: UFW outbound connections are configured
rules.explanation: Configure firewall rules for new outbound connections. Note: • Changing firewall settings while connected over the network may lock you out of the system. • Unlike iptables, when a new outbound rule is added, ufw automatically handles related established connections, so no rules for the latter type are required.
rules.impact: If rules for new outbound connections are missing, all packets will be dropped by the default policy, preventing network use.

rules.title: UFW firewall rules exist for all open ports
rules.explanation: Services and ports can be allowed or explicitly denied. Note: • Changing firewall settings while connected over the network may lock you out of the system. • The remediation command opens the port to traffic from all sources. Review the ufw documentation and apply any restrictions in accordance with site policy.
rules.impact: To reduce the system's attack surface, all services and ports should be blocked unless they are required. • Any ports open on non-loopback addresses need firewall rules to control traffic. • If a firewall rule is not configured for open ports, the default firewall policy will drop all packets to those ports. • For required ports, a firewall rule should be created that allows approved connections according to local site policy. • For unapproved ports, an explicit deny rule should be created.

rules.title: UFW default deny firewall policy is set
rules.explanation: A default-deny connection policy ensures that any unconfigured network use is rejected. Note: Any port or protocol without an explicit allow before the default deny will be blocked.
rules.impact: With a default-accept policy, the firewall accepts any packet for which a deny rule is not configured. It is easier to whitelist acceptable use than to blacklist unacceptable use.

rules.title: Nftables is installed
rules.explanation: nftables provides a new in-kernel packet classification framework based on a network-specific virtual machine (VM) and a new userspace command-line tool, nft. nftables reuses existing Netfilter subsystems, such as the existing hook infrastructure, connection tracking, NAT, and the userspace queuing and logging subsystems. Notes: • nftables is available in Linux kernel 3.13 and later. • Only one firewall utility should be installed and configured. • Changing firewall settings over a network connection may lock you out of the system.
rules.impact: nftables is a Linux kernel subsystem that can protect against threats originating from the corporate network, including malicious mobile code and poorly configured software on the host.

rules.title: UFW is removed or disabled with nftables
rules.explanation: A single host firewall implementation is expected, with a default deny policy, loopback traffic allowed and a rule set that is loaded at boot. Mixing ufw, nftables and iptables produces rules whose evaluation order is hard to reason about.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Iptables is flushed using nftables
rules.explanation: nftables is a replacement for iptables, ip6tables, ebtables, and arptables.
rules.impact: iptables and nftables can be mixed. However, this increases complexity and the likelihood of errors. For simplicity, remove all iptables rules and ensure that it is not loaded.

rules.title: The nftables table exists
rules.explanation: Tables hold chains. Each table has only one address family and applies only to packets of that family. Tables may have one of five families.
rules.impact: nftables has no default tables. Without a table, nftables will not filter network traffic.

rules.title: Nftables base chains exist
rules.explanation: Chains are containers for rules. There are two kinds: base chains and regular chains. A base chain is the entry point for packets from the network stack; a regular chain can be used as a jump target and is used for better organization of rules.
rules.impact: If a base chain with a hook for input, forward, and drop does not exist, packets that would pass through these chains will not be affected by nftables.

rules.title: Nftables loopback traffic is configured
rules.explanation: Configure the loopback interface to accept traffic. Configure all other interfaces to deny traffic to the loopback network.
rules.impact: Loopback traffic is generated between processes on the computer and is typically critical to system operation. The loopback interface is the only place where loopback network traffic should be seen. All other interfaces should ignore traffic for this network as a spoofing protection measure.

rules.title: Nftables outbound and established connections are configured
rules.explanation: A single host firewall implementation is expected, with a default deny policy, loopback traffic allowed and a rule set that is loaded at boot. Mixing ufw, nftables and iptables produces rules whose evaluation order is hard to reason about.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Nftables default firewall policy is deny
rules.explanation: The base chain policy is the default verdict applied to packets that reach the end of the chain.
rules.impact: There are two policies: accept (default) and drop. If the policy is set to accept, the firewall accepts any packet for which a deny rule is not configured, and the packet continues through the network stack. It is easier to whitelist acceptable use than to blacklist unacceptable use. Note: Changing firewall settings while connected over the network may lock you out of the system.

rules.title: The nftables service is enabled
rules.explanation: The nftables service allows nftables rule sets to be loaded at boot or when the nftables service starts.
rules.impact: The nftables service restores nftables rules from the rule files specified in /etc/nftables.conf during boot or when the nftables service starts.

rules.title: Nftables rules are persistent
rules.explanation: nftables is a Linux kernel subsystem that provides filtering and classification of network packets/datagrams/frames. The nftables service reads /etc/nftables.conf for the nftables file or files to include in the nftables ruleset. An nftables ruleset containing base input, forward, and output chains allows network traffic to be filtered.
rules.impact: Changes made to the nftables ruleset affect only the running system; you also need to configure the nftables ruleset to apply at boot.

rules.title: Iptables packages are installed
rules.explanation: iptables is a utility that allows a system administrator to configure the tables provided by the Linux kernel firewall, implemented as various Netfilter modules, as well as the chains and rules it stores. Different kernel modules and programs are used for different protocols; iptables applies to IPv4, ip6tables to IPv6, arptables to ARP, and ebtables to Ethernet frames.
rules.impact: A method for configuring and maintaining firewall rules is required to configure a host-based firewall.

rules.title: Nftables is not installed together with iptables
rules.explanation: nftables is a Linux kernel subsystem that provides filtering and classification of network packets/datagrams/frames and is the successor to iptables.
rules.impact: Using iptables and nftables together can cause conflicts.

rules.title: UFW is removed or disabled with iptables
rules.explanation: A single host firewall implementation is expected, with a default deny policy, loopback traffic allowed and a rule set that is loaded at boot. Mixing ufw, nftables and iptables produces rules whose evaluation order is hard to reason about.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Iptables default firewall policy is deny
rules.explanation: A default deny-all connections policy ensures that any unconfigured network use is rejected. Notes: • Changing firewall settings while connected over the network may lock you out of the system. • Remediation will affect only the active system firewall; be sure to configure the default policy in firewall management so that it also applies at boot.
rules.impact: With a default-accept policy, the firewall accepts any packet for which a deny rule is not configured. It is easier to whitelist acceptable use than to blacklist unacceptable use.

rules.title: Iptables loopback traffic is configured
rules.explanation: Configure the loopback interface to accept traffic. Configure all other interfaces to deny traffic to the loopback network (127.0.0.0/8). Note: • Changing firewall settings while connected over the network may result in being locked out of the system. • Remediation will affect only the active system firewall; be sure to configure the default policy in firewall management so that it also applies at boot.
rules.impact: Loopback traffic is generated between processes on the computer and is typically critical to system operation. The loopback interface is the only place where loopback network traffic (127.0.0.0/8) should be visible. All other interfaces should ignore traffic on this network as a spoofing protection measure.
