rules.title: Permissions on /etc/ssh/sshd_config are configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/ssh/sshd_config file controls SSH daemon behavior, including authentication and access settings. Restrictive ownership and mode limit who can read or change that policy.
rules.impact: Although the system may not have user jobs that need to run, the system has maintenance jobs that may include security monitoring that needs to run. If another task-scheduling method is not used, cron is used to run them and should be enabled and running.

rules.title: Permissions on SSH host private key files are configured
rules.explanation: These files define users, groups, passwords and shells. Excess permissions let an unprivileged user read or replace them and take over the host.
rules.impact: This file contains information about which system jobs are executed by cron. Write access to these files may give unprivileged users an opportunity to elevate their privileges. Read access to these files may give users insight into the system jobs that are running on the system and provide them an opportunity to obtain unauthorized privileged access.

rules.title: Permissions on SSH host public key files are configured
rules.explanation: These files define users, groups, passwords and shells. Excess permissions let an unprivileged user read or replace them and take over the host.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.title: SSH access is configured
rules.explanation: sshd directives such as AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers, and DenyGroups restrict which accounts may authenticate over SSH.
rules.impact: Without explicit access restrictions, all local accounts—including service accounts—may accept SSH logins, expanding remote compromise paths.

rules.title: The SSH banner is configured
rules.explanation: The SSH Banner setting displays a message before authentication. It is typically used to present an authorized-access warning.
rules.impact: An authorized-access banner supports compliance expectations and clarifies that unauthorized use of the system is prohibited.
rules.scope: See section 4.2.5 in CentOS Linux 7 v4.0.0 (Audit/Remediation).

rules.title: SSH ciphers are configured
rules.explanation: The sshd Ciphers setting selects encryption algorithms used to protect SSH session confidentiality after key exchange.
rules.impact: Weak or legacy ciphers increase the risk that intercepted SSH traffic can be decrypted, exposing session contents and credentials.
rules.scope: See section 4.2.6 in CentOS Linux 7 v4.0.0 (Audit/Remediation).

rules.title: SSH ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured
rules.explanation: ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax control how the SSH server detects and terminates idle or unresponsive client sessions through keepalive messages.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.
rules.scope: See section 4.2.7 in CentOS Linux 7 v4.0.0 (Audit/Remediation).

rules.title: SSH DisableForwarding is enabled
rules.explanation: DisableForwarding disables SSH forwarding features such as TCP port forwarding, X11 forwarding, and agent forwarding in a single control.
rules.impact: On many systems, only the system administrator is authorized to schedule cron jobs. Using the cron.allow file to control who can run cron jobs enforces this policy. It is easier to manage an allow list than a deny list. On a deny list, you may add a user ID to the system and forget to add it to the deny files.
rules.scope: See section 4.2.8 in CentOS Linux 7 v4.0.0 (Audit/Remediation).

rules.title: SSH GSSAPIAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: GSSAPIAuthentication enables Kerberos/GSSAPI-based SSH authentication. It is typically needed only in environments that use that infrastructure.
rules.impact: On many systems, only the system administrator is authorized to schedule jobs. Using the at.allow file to control who can run jobs enforces this policy. An allow list is easier to manage than a deny list. With a deny list, you could potentially add a user ID to the system and forget to add it to the deny files.
rules.scope: See section 4.2.9 in CentOS Linux 7 v4.0.0 (Audit/Remediation).

rules.title: SSH HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: HostbasedAuthentication trusts remote hosts based on host identity rather than verifying individual users with keys or passwords.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: IgnoreRhosts causes sshd to ignore .rhosts and .shosts files as authentication sources. Those legacy trust files are insecure by modern standards.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH KexAlgorithms is configured
rules.explanation: The KexAlgorithms offered by sshd are restricted to the modern set so that weak or deprecated cryptography cannot be negotiated with the server.
rules.impact: Using weak key-exchange algorithms may allow an attacker to intercept or decrypt an SSH connection. Only strong algorithms should be used.
rules.scope: See section 4.2.12 in CentOS Linux 7 v4.0.0 (Audit/Remediation).

rules.title: SSH LoginGraceTime is configured
rules.explanation: LoginGraceTime limits how long an unauthenticated SSH connection may remain open while authentication is attempted.
rules.impact: A timeout that is too long can make the server vulnerable to brute-force attacks, while one that is too short may interfere with legitimate users. Balance is important for security.

rules.title: SSH LogLevel is configured
rules.explanation: The sshd LogLevel setting controls the detail of authentication and session events written to logs (commonly VERBOSE or INFO).
rules.impact: An adequate logging level is required for auditing, security monitoring, and incident investigation. A level that is too low may not provide sufficient information for analysis.

rules.title: SSH MACs are configured
rules.explanation: The MACs offered by sshd are restricted to the modern set so that weak or deprecated cryptography cannot be negotiated with the server.
rules.impact: Use of weak MAC algorithms may allow an attacker to modify data in transit. Only strong algorithms should be used.
rules.scope: See section 4.2.15 in CentOS Linux 7 v4.0.0 (Audit/Remediation).

rules.title: SSH MaxAuthTries is configured
rules.explanation: MaxAuthTries limits the number of authentication attempts permitted per SSH connection.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH MaxSessions is configured
rules.explanation: MaxSessions limits the number of multiplexed sessions that may be opened over a single SSH connection.
rules.impact: Limiting the number of sessions prevents resource abuse and reduces potential damage if an account is compromised.
rules.scope: See section 4.2.17 in CentOS Linux 7 v4.0.0 (Audit/Remediation).

rules.title: SSH MaxStartups is configured
rules.explanation: MaxStartups limits concurrent unauthenticated SSH connections, protecting the daemon from connection floods before authentication completes.
rules.impact: This helps prevent denial-of-service (DoS) attacks by limiting the number of connections the server must handle concurrently before authentication.

rules.title: SSH PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitEmptyPasswords controls whether accounts with empty password strings may authenticate over SSH.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH PermitRootLogin is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitRootLogin controls whether the root account may authenticate directly over SSH. Administrative access is preferably obtained via individual accounts and privilege elevation.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitUserEnvironment allows users to set environment variables through files such as ~/.ssh/environment that sshd will apply at login.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: SSH UsePAM is enabled
rules.explanation: UsePAM causes sshd to authenticate and establish sessions through the PAM stack, integrating password policy, account locks, and related controls.
rules.impact: Disabling UsePAM bypasses PAM-based password policy, lockout, and multifactor controls for SSH authentication.

rules.title: Sudo is installed
rules.explanation: sudo allows a permitted user to execute a command as the superuser or another user, as specified by the security policy. The real (not effective) user ID of the calling user is used to determine the user name with which to query the security policy.
rules.impact: sudo supports a plugin architecture for security policy and I/O logging. Third parties can develop and distribute their own policy and I/O logging plugins to work seamlessly with the sudo interface. The default security policy is sudoers, which is configured via the /etc/sudoers file and any entries in /etc/sudoers.d. The security policy determines what privileges (if any) a user has to run sudo. The policy may require users to authenticate with a password or another authentication mechanism. If authentication is required, sudo will terminate if the user password is not entered within a configurable timeout. This restriction is policy-dependent.

rules.title: Sudo commands use pty
rules.explanation: sudo can be configured to run only from a pseudo-terminal (pseudo-pty).
rules.impact: Attackers can use sudo to launch a malicious program that will spawn a background process that remains even after the main program finishes executing.

rules.title: The sudo log file exists
rules.explanation: sudo can use its own log file
rules.impact: The sudo log file simplifies auditing of sudo commands.

rules.title: Users must provide a password to elevate privileges
rules.explanation: Ensure that users must provide a password to elevate privileges.
rules.impact: Restricting which users can remotely access the system via SSH will help ensure that only authorized users have access to the system.

rules.title: Re-authentication for privilege escalation is not disabled globally
rules.explanation: Ensure that re-authentication for privilege elevation is not disabled globally.
rules.impact: SSH provides several logging levels with varying degrees of detail. DEBUG is strongly discouraged except strictly for debugging SSH communications, because it provides so much data that it is difficult to identify important security information. INFO is the baseline level that records only SSH user login activity. In many situations, such as incident response, it is important to determine when a particular user was active on the system. A logout record can eliminate those users who have disconnected, which helps narrow the field.

rules.title: The sudo authentication timeout is configured correctly
rules.explanation: Ensure that the sudo authentication timeout is configured correctly
rules.impact: If the usePAM parameter is set to yes, PAM correctly works with account and session types. This is important if you want to restrict access to services based on IP, time, or other account factors. In addition, you can ensure that users inherit certain environment variables at logon or deny access to the server.

rules.title: Access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command allows a user to run a command or shell as another user. The program has been superseded by sudo, which provides more granular control over privileged access. Typically, the su command can be executed by any user. By uncommenting the pam_wheel.so statement in the /etc/pam.d/su file, the su command will allow only users in specified groups to execute su. This group should be empty to reinforce the use of sudo for privileged access.
rules.impact: Restricting use of su and using sudo instead allows system administrators to better control user privilege elevation for executing privileged commands. The sudo utility also provides a better logging and auditing mechanism because it can log every command executed via sudo, whereas su can only record that the user executed the su program.

rules.title: The latest pam version is installed
rules.explanation: Updated PAM versions include additional features.
rules.impact: To ensure full system functionality and access to the options covered by this benchmark, the latest version of libpam-runtime must be installed on the system.

rules.title: Libpam-modules is installed
rules.explanation: Pluggable authentication modules for PAM
rules.impact: Ensure full system functionality and access to the PAM options covered by this benchmark.

rules.title: Libpam-pwquality is installed
rules.explanation: libpwquality provides common functions for checking password quality and scoring passwords based on their apparent randomness. The library also provides a function for generating random passwords with good pronounceability. This module can be stacked in the password stack of a given service to enforce password strength checks. The code was originally based on the pam_cracklib module, and this module is backward compatible with its options.
rules.impact: Strong passwords reduce the risk of brute-force compromise.

rules.title: The pam_unix module is enabled
rules.explanation: pam_unix is the standard Unix authentication module. It uses standard calls from system libraries to retrieve and set account information and to authenticate. This is typically obtained from the /etc/passwd file and, if shadow is enabled, also from the /etc/shadow file. The account component performs the task of establishing the user's account and password status based on the following shadow items: expire, last_change, max_change, min_change, warn_change. In the latter case it may prompt the user with advice to change the password or, by returning PAM_AUTHTOKEN_REQD, delay granting the service to the user until they set a new password. The entries listed above are described on the shadow(5) man page. If a user entry does not contain one or more of these records, the corresponding shadow check is not performed. The authentication component performs the task of verifying the user's credentials (password). The default action of this module is not to allow the user access to the service if their official password is empty.
rules.impact: The system must grant access only after the user is authenticated.

rules.title: The pam_faillock module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_faillock.so module stores a list of failed authentication attempts for each user during a specified interval and locks the account if the number of consecutive failed authentications exceeds the configured value (this is determined by the Deny parameter in the Faillock configuration). It stores failure records in per-user files in the Tally directory.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: The pam_pwquality module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_pwquality.so module performs password quality checking. This module can be stacked in the password stack of a given service to enforce password strength checking. The code was originally based on the pam_cracklib module, and this module is backward compatible with its options. The action of this module is to prompt the user for a password and check its strength against the system dictionary and a set of rules to identify poor choices. The first action is to prompt for a single password, check its strength, and then, if it is considered strong, prompt for the password a second time (to ensure it was entered correctly the first time). If all is well, the password is passed to subsequent modules to be set as the new authentication token.
rules.impact: Without pam_pwquality in the password stack, users may set weak passwords that are easier to guess or crack.

rules.title: The pam_pwhistory module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_pwhistory.so module stores the last passwords for each user in order to enforce password change history and prevent the user from changing to the same password too frequently. This module does not work together with Kerberos. In general, using this module together with NIS or LDAP is of little value, because old passwords are stored on the local machine and are not available on another machine for password history checks.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Lockout after failed password attempts is configured
rules.explanation: The deny setting in faillock configuration defines how many consecutive failed authentications trigger an account lock.
rules.impact: Appropriate lockout thresholds slow online password-guessing attacks against local authentication services.

rules.title: Password unlock time is configured
rules.explanation: unlock_time=<n> - Access will be restored after a number of seconds following lockout. A value of 0 has the same meaning as never: access will not be restored without resetting faillock records using the faillock(8) command. Note: • The default directory used by pam_faillock is typically cleared at system boot, so access will also be re-enabled after a system reboot. If this is undesirable, a different directory must be set with the dir parameter. • Permanently locking users is generally undesirable because they can easily become the target of a denial-of-service attack unless usernames are random and kept secret from potential attackers. • The maximum configurable value for unlock_time is 604800.
rules.impact: Sufficient unlock delays make repeated online guessing impractical while still allowing eventual recovery of legitimate accounts.

rules.title: Failed password attempt lockout includes the root account
rules.explanation: Ensure that failed password attempt lockout includes the root account.
rules.impact: Including the root account in the lockout policy prevents brute-force attacks against the most privileged account on the system.

rules.title: The number of changed characters in the password is configured
rules.explanation: Ensure that the number of changed characters in the password is configured.
rules.impact: Requiring a minimum number of changed characters ensures that new passwords differ substantially from old ones rather than being minor variations.

rules.title: Minimum password length is configured
rules.explanation: Minimum password length requirements ensure newly set passwords contain enough characters to provide adequate entropy against guessing attacks.
rules.impact: Short passwords are substantially easier to brute-force. Enforcing sufficient length is a primary control for password strength.

rules.title: Password complexity is configured
rules.explanation: Password complexity can be set using: • minclass — the minimum number of character classes required in a new password (digits, uppercase, lowercase, and other). For example, minclass = 4 requires digits, uppercase and lowercase letters, and special characters. • dcredit — Maximum credit for the number of digits in a new password. If less than 0, this is the minimum number of digits in the new password. For example, dcredit = -1 requires at least one digit. • ucredit — Maximum credit for uppercase characters in a new password. If less than 0, this is the minimum number of uppercase characters in the new password. For example, ucredit = -1 requires at least one uppercase character. • ocredit — Maximum credit for other characters in a new password. If less than 0, this is the minimum number of other characters in the new password. For example, ocredit = -1 requires at least one special character. • lcredit — Maximum credit for lowercase characters in a new password. If less than 0, this is the minimum number of lowercase characters in the new password. For example, lcredit = -1 requires at least one lowercase character.
rules.impact: Strong passwords protect systems from being compromised by brute-force methods. Requiring at least one non-alphabetic character increases the search space beyond simple dictionary words, making the resulting password harder to crack. Forcing users to choose an overly complex password, e.g. some combination of uppercase and lowercase letters, digits, and special characters, has a negative effect. It imposes additional burden on users, and many of them will use predictable patterns (for example, a capital letter in the first position, followed by lowercase letters, then one or two digits and a "special character" at the end). Attackers know this, so dictionary attacks will often contain these common patterns and use the most common substitutions, such as $ for s, @ for a, 1 for l, 0 for o.

rules.title: Consecutive identical password characters are configured
rules.explanation: Ensure that consecutive identical password characters are configured.
rules.impact: Restricting sequential characters prevents use of easily guessed passwords such as "aaaAAA111".

rules.title: The maximum number of consecutive password characters is configured
rules.explanation: Password ageing and quality settings are enforced through the PAM stack and /etc/login.defs. Weak or unmanaged passwords are the most common way into a host.
rules.impact: This prevents the use of passwords that are merely character sequences, making them more resistant to attacks.

rules.title: Password dictionary checking is enabled
rules.explanation: Dictionary checking compares candidate passwords against lists of common or compromised passwords before accepting a change.
rules.impact: Dictionary checking prevents the use of common words or simple variations that are easy to guess in dictionary attacks.

rules.title: Password quality checking is enabled
rules.explanation: Enforcement options for pam_pwquality require password quality checks to be applied rather than treated as optional warnings.
rules.impact: Without enforcement of a password quality policy, users may bypass password complexity requirements.

rules.title: Password quality is applied for the root user
rules.explanation: Ensure that password quality is applied for the root user.
rules.impact: The root account is the most privileged, so it is especially important that its password is strong and complies with security policies.

rules.title: Password history remembering is configured
rules.explanation: The remember setting for pam_pwhistory defines how many previous passwords are retained and rejected on reuse.
rules.impact: Remembering password history prevents a user from cycling through a small set of passwords.

rules.title: Password history is enabled for the root user
rules.explanation: enforce_for_root for pam_pwhistory applies password-history restrictions to the root account as well as ordinary users.
rules.impact: Enforcing password history for root prevents reuse of old passwords for the most privileged account.

rules.title: Pam_pwhistory includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: The use_authtok option tells pam_pwhistory to use the password token already obtained earlier in the PAM stack rather than prompting again.
rules.impact: This ensures the PAM module stack works correctly and that password history checking is performed on the correct password.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not contain nullok
rules.explanation: The nullok argument overrides the default action of pam_unix.so, which denies a user access to a service if their official password is empty.
rules.impact: Using a strong password is necessary to protect personal and confidential information from unauthorized access.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include remember
rules.explanation: The remember option in pam_unix is a legacy password-history mechanism superseded by pam_pwhistory.
rules.impact: Using the correct module for password history functionality ensures proper operation and security.

rules.title: Pam_unix uses a strong password hashing algorithm
rules.explanation: pam_unix hashing options select algorithms such as yescrypt, SHA-512, or bcrypt for storing local password hashes.
rules.impact: Using a strong hashing algorithm (such as yescrypt) is critical to protecting passwords against brute-force attacks if the password file is leaked.

rules.title: Pam_unix includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: use_authtok — during a password change, force the module to set the new password to the one provided by a previously stacked password module.
rules.impact: use_authtok allows multiple PAM modules to confirm the new password before it is accepted.

rules.title: Password lifetime is configured
rules.explanation: The PASS_MAX_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to force passwords to expire after they reach a certain age. PASS_MAX_DAYS <N> is the maximum number of days a password may be used. If the password is older than this, a password change will be forced. If not specified, -1 is assumed (which disables the restriction).
rules.impact: The window of opportunity for an attacker to use compromised credentials, or to successfully compromise credentials via an online brute-force attack, is limited by the password expiration period. Thus, reducing the maximum password lifetime also reduces the attacker's window of opportunity. We recommend changing the password annually. This is primarily because, despite their best intentions, users will reuse credentials across accounts. Thus, even if a breach is publicly disclosed, the user may not see that notice or may forget that they have an account on that site. This can leave shared credentials vulnerable indefinitely. Having an organizational policy that requires password expiration within 1 year (annually) is a reasonable compromise to mitigate this issue with minimal user burden.

rules.title: The minimum password lifetime is configured
rules.explanation: The minimum password age defines the number of days a password must be used before it can be changed. PASS_MIN_DAYS <N> is the minimum number of days allowed between password changes. Any attempt to change the password before this time will be rejected. If not specified, 0 is assumed (which disables the restriction).
rules.impact: Users may have favorite passwords that they like to use because they are easy to remember and they believe the chosen password is protected against compromise. Unfortunately, passwords are compromised, and if an attacker targets a specific individual user's account, then, with prior knowledge about that user, reuse of old, potentially compromised passwords may lead to a security breach. By restricting how frequently a password can be changed, an administrator can prevent users from repeatedly changing their password in an attempt to circumvent password reuse controls.

rules.title: Password expiration warning days are configured
rules.explanation: PASS_WARN_AGE in /etc/login.defs defines how many days before expiration users are warned to change their passwords.
rules.impact: Adequate warning reduces abrupt lockouts and unsafe ad-hoc recovery practices when passwords expire unexpectedly.

rules.title: A strong password hashing algorithm is configured
rules.explanation: ENCRYPT_METHOD in /etc/login.defs selects the default hashing algorithm used when new local passwords are created.
rules.impact: Strong hashing algorithms increase the cost of offline cracking if password hashes are obtained from the system.

rules.title: Inactive password lock is configured
rules.explanation: User accounts that have been inactive for a specified period of time can be disabled automatically. INACTIVE defines the number of days after the password maximum lifetime is reached during which the user must replace that password. The value is stored in the shadow password file. Entering 0 will disable an expired password without delay. Entering -1 will clear the corresponding field in the shadow password file.
rules.impact: Inactive accounts pose a system security threat because users do not log on to notice failed logon attempts or other anomalies.

rules.title: The last password change date for all users is already in the past
rules.explanation: Ensure that the last password change date for all users is already in the past.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: Root is the only account with UID 0
rules.explanation: Any account with UID 0 has superuser privileges on the system.
rules.impact: This access should be restricted to the root account by default and only from the system console. Administrative access should be performed through an unprivileged account using an approved mechanism, as specified in section 5.6. Ensure that access to the su command is restricted.

rules.title: Root is the only account with GID 0
rules.explanation: The usermod command can be used to specify which group the root account belongs to. This affects access rights to files created by the root account.
rules.impact: Using GID 0 for the root account helps prevent unprivileged users from accidentally accessing files owned by root.

rules.title: The root group is the only group with GID 0
rules.explanation: The groupmod command can be used to specify which group the root group belongs to. This affects permissions on files owned by the root group.
rules.impact: Using GID 0 for the root group helps prevent accidental access by unprivileged users to files owned by the root group.

rules.title: The root password is set
rules.explanation: There are several ways to access the root account directly. Without a password set, any user can gain access and thereby control the entire system.
rules.impact: Access to root must always be protected.
rules.scope: See section 4.5.2.4 in CentOS Linux 7 v4.0.0 (Audit/Remediation).

rules.title: Integrity of the root PATH
rules.explanation: The root user can execute any command on the system and can be tricked into unintentionally running a program if PATH is set incorrectly.
rules.impact: Including the current working directory (.) or another writable directory in the root user's executable path increases the likelihood that an attacker can obtain superuser access by causing an administrator running as root to execute a "Trojan horse" program.

rules.title: Root user umask is configured
rules.explanation: The user file-creation mode mask (umask) is used to determine access permissions for newly created directories and files. On Linux, the default permissions for any newly created directory are 0777 (rwxrwxrwx), and for any newly created file are 0666 (rw-rw-rw-). umask modifies the default Linux permissions by restricting (masking) those permissions. The mask is not simply subtracted; it is processed bitwise. Bits set in the umask are cleared in the resulting file mode. umask can be set with octal or symbolic values: • Octal (numeric) value — represented by three or four digits, i.e. umask 0027 or umask 027. If a four-digit umask is used, the first digit is ignored. The remaining three digits affect the resulting permissions for user, group, and world/other respectively. • Symbolic value — represented by a comma-separated list for user u, group g, and world/other o. The listed permissions are not masked by umask. i.e. the mask set with umask u=rwx,g=rx,o= is the symbolic equivalent of octal umask 027. This umask will set a newly created directory to file mode drwxr-x--- and a newly created file to file mode rw-r-----. Root user shell configuration files: • /root/.bash_profile — executed to configure the root user's shell before the initial command prompt. Read only by login shells. • /root/.bashrc — executed for interactive shells. Read only by a shell that is both interactive and non-login. umask is set in priority order. If umask is set in multiple places, this priority order will determine the system default umask. The priority order is: 1. /root/.bash_profile 2. /root/.bashrc 3. System default umask.
rules.impact: Setting a secure umask value ensures that users make a deliberate choice of file access permissions. A permissive umask value may result in directories or files with excessive permissions that can be read and/or written by unauthorized users.

rules.title: System accounts do not have a valid login shell
rules.explanation: System accounts are intended to run services rather than interactive logins and should use non-login shells such as /usr/sbin/nologin or /bin/false.
rules.impact: Assigning an invalid login shell to system accounts prevents their use for interactive logon, reducing the attack surface.

rules.title: Accounts without a valid login shell are locked
rules.explanation: Accounts assigned a non-login shell should also have locked passwords so authentication cannot succeed through alternate PAM entry points.
rules.impact: Locking such accounts adds an additional layer of security by preventing any login attempts even if the password is known.

rules.title: Nologin is not listed in the /etc/shells file
rules.explanation: /etc/shells is a text file that contains the full path names of valid login shells. This file is used by the chsh command and is available for query by other programs. Be aware that some programs consult this file to determine whether a user is a regular user; for example, FTP daemons traditionally deny access to users whose shells are not listed in this file.
rules.impact: A user can use chsh to change the configured shell. If a user is configured with a shell that is not listed in /etc/shells, the system assumes the account is restricted in some way. For chsh, this means the user cannot change that value. Other programs may query this list and apply similar restrictions. By placing nologin in /etc/shells, any user whose shell is nologin is treated as a full, unrestricted user. This is not the expected behavior for nologin.

rules.title: Default user shell timeout is configured
rules.explanation: The TMOUT setting defines an idle timeout after which interactive shells automatically exit.
rules.impact: Idle shell timeouts reduce the window during which an unattended terminal session can be abused without re-authentication.

rules.title: The default user mask is configured
rules.explanation: The user file-creation mode mask (umask) is used to determine the access permissions of newly created directories and files. In Linux, the default permissions for any newly created directory are 0777 (rwxrwxrwx), and for any newly created file are 0666 (rw-rw-rw-). umask changes the Linux default permissions by restricting (masking) those permissions. The mask is not simply subtracted; it is processed bitwise. Bits that are set in umask are cleared in the resulting file mode. umask can be set with octal or symbolic values: • Octal (numeric) value — represented by three or four digits, e.g. umask 0027 or umask 027. If a four-digit mask is used, the first digit is ignored. The remaining three digits affect the resulting permissions for user, group, and world/other respectively. • Symbolic value — represented by a comma-separated list for user u, group g, and world/other o. The listed permissions are not masked by umask. For example, a mask set with umask u=rwx,g=rx,o= is the symbolic equivalent of octal mask 027. This mask will set a newly created directory to file mode drwxr-x--- and a newly created file to file mode rw-r-----. The default mask can be configured using the pam_umask module or in a system-wide shell configuration file. A user who creates directories or files may, at their discretion, change permissions with the chmod command or choose a different default umask by adding a umask command to a user shell configuration file (.bash_profile or .bashrc) in their home directory. Setting the default umask: • pam_umask module: o will set umask according to the system default in /etc/login.defs and user settings, addressing the problem of different umask settings for different shells, display managers, remote sessions, etc. o The umask=<mask> value in /etc/login.defs is interpreted as octal o Setting USERGROUPS_ENAB to yes in /etc/login.defs (the default): ▪ will allow the group umask bits to be set the same as the owner bits (examples: 022 -> 002, 077 -> 007) for non-root users if uid matches gid and the username matches <primary group name>. ▪ userdel will remove the user's group if it has no remaining members, and useradd will create a default group named after the user. • System-wide shell configuration file: o /etc/profile — used to set system-wide environment variables in user shells. Sometimes the variables are the same as in .bash_profile; however, this file is used to set the initial PATH or PS1 for all system shell users. It is executed only for interactive login shells or shells invoked with the --login option. o /etc/profile.d — /etc/profile will execute scripts from /etc/profile.d/*.sh. It is recommended to place your configuration in a shell script in /etc/profile.d to set your own system-wide environment variables. o /etc/bashrc — the system-wide version of .bashrc. On Fedora-derived distributions, /etc/bashrc also invokes /etc/profile.d/*.sh if the shell is not a login shell, but redirects output to /dev/null if it is non-interactive. It is executed only for interactive shells or if BASH_ENV is set to /etc/bashrc. User shell configuration files: • ~/.bash_profile — executed to configure the shell before the initial command prompt. Read only by login shells. • ~/.bashrc — executed for interactive shells; read only by a shell that is both interactive and non-login. umask is applied in priority order. If umask is set in multiple places, this priority order determines the system default umask. Priority order: 1. A file in /etc/profile.d/ ending in .sh. This overrides any other system-wide umask settings. 2. In /etc/profile 3. In the pam_umask.so module in /etc/pam.d/postlogin 4. In /etc/login.defs 5. In /etc/default/login.
rules.impact: Setting a secure default umask value ensures that users make a conscious choice about file access permissions. A permissive umask value can result in directories or files with excessive permissions that can be read and/or written by unauthorized users.

rules.title: AIDE is installed
rules.explanation: AIDE takes a snapshot of file system state, including modification times, permissions, and file hashes, which can then be compared with the current file system state to detect system changes.
rules.impact: By monitoring file system state, compromised files can be detected to prevent or limit the impact of accidental or malicious misconfigurations or modified binaries.

rules.title: Regular filesystem integrity checking
rules.explanation: Periodic file system integrity checking is required to detect changes in the file system.
rules.impact: Periodic file integrity checking allows the system administrator to regularly determine whether critical files have been modified in an unauthorized manner.

rules.title: Cryptographic mechanisms are used to protect the integrity of audit tools
rules.explanation: Ensure that cryptographic mechanisms are used to protect the integrity of audit tools.
rules.impact: The /etc/group file should be protected from unauthorized modification by unprivileged users, but should be readable because this information is used by many unprivileged programs.

rules.title: The journald service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: systemd-journald collects and stores system journal logs, including service, kernel, and authentication-related events on Ubuntu systems.
rules.impact: Without an active journald service, important security and operational events may not be recorded for detection and investigation.

rules.title: Access to the journal log file is configured
rules.explanation: Ensure that access to the journal log file is configured.
rules.impact: Correct permissions prevent unauthorized reading or modification of log files, which may contain sensitive information.

rules.title: Journal log file rotation is configured
rules.explanation: Ensure that journal log file rotation is configured.
rules.impact: Configuring rotation prevents log files from exhausting disk space and ensures logs are retained for an adequate period for audit purposes.

rules.title: ForwardToSyslog logging is disabled
rules.explanation: The setting is turned off so that the feature it enables cannot be used against the host.
rules.impact: If only the systemd journal is used, duplicating logs to syslog can cause excessive resource use and complicate log management.

rules.title: Journal storage is configured
rules.explanation: Ensure that journal storage is configured.
rules.impact: Correct journal storage configuration ensures that logs are retained appropriately for audit and debugging purposes.

rules.title: Journald compression is configured
rules.explanation: journald can compress stored journal data to reduce disk usage while retaining more history within available space.
rules.impact: Enabling compression allows more log data to be stored in the same amount of disk space, which is useful for long-term audit.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-remote is installed
rules.explanation: systemd-journal-remote supports sending the journal events it collects to a remote journal host or receiving messages from remote hosts, which enables centralized log management.
rules.impact: Storing log data on a remote host protects log integrity from local attacks. If an attacker obtains root access on the local system, they can forge or delete log data stored locally.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-remote authentication is configured
rules.explanation: Ensure that systemd-journal-remote authentication is configured.
rules.impact: Configuring authentication prevents unauthorized transmission or receipt of log data, which could lead to information disclosure or log tampering.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-upload is enabled and active
rules.explanation: systemd-journal-upload forwards local journal entries to a remote journal collector for centralized retention and analysis.
rules.impact: An active, running log forwarding service ensures that logs are collected centrally for security monitoring and audit.

rules.title: The systemd-journal-remote service is not in use
rules.explanation: systemd-journal-remote can accept journal data from remote hosts. Hosts that are not designated log collectors should not expose this service.
rules.impact: If this functionality is not required, the service should be disabled to reduce the attack surface and prevent unauthorized receipt of data.

rules.title: Access to all log files is configured
rules.explanation: Files under /var/log should use restrictive modes and ownership so unprivileged users cannot read or alter sensitive log content.
rules.impact: World-readable logs can disclose usernames, timestamps, errors, and other details useful for reconnaissance and privilege escalation.
rules.scope: Log files in /var/log/ and their permissions.

rules.title: Auditd packages are installed
rules.explanation: auditd is the userspace component of the Linux audit system. It is responsible for writing audit records to disk.
rules.impact: Without audit packages, kernel-level security event collection required for many compliance and investigation use cases is unavailable.

rules.title: The auditd service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: Enable the Auditd daemon to record system events.
rules.impact: A stopped auditd daemon leaves the system without active audit logging of privileged and security-relevant activity.

rules.title: Auditing for processes that start before auditd is enabled
rules.explanation: The kernel audit=1 parameter enables auditing early in boot so events that occur before auditd starts can still be captured.
rules.impact: Without early audit enablement, initialization activity may go unrecorded, reducing visibility into pre-auditd compromise techniques.

rules.title: Audit_backlog_limit is sufficient
rules.explanation: In the kernel-level audit subsystem, a socket buffer queue is used to store audit events. Whenever a new audit event is received, it is recorded and prepared for addition to this queue. The kernel boot parameter Audit_backlog_limit=N, where N represents the number of messages, ensures that the queue cannot exceed a specified size. If an audit event is recorded that would cause the queue to grow beyond this limit, a failure occurs that is handled according to the system configuration.
rules.impact: If an audit event is recorded that causes the queue to grow beyond Audit_backlog_limit, a failure occurs, audit records are lost, and potentially malicious activity may go unnoticed.

rules.title: Audit log storage size is configured
rules.explanation: Configure the maximum audit log file size. Once the log reaches the maximum size, it is rotated and a new log file is created.
rules.impact: It is important to define an appropriate log file size so that logs do not impact the system or lose audit data.

rules.title: Audit logs are not deleted automatically
rules.explanation: Ensure that audit logs are not deleted automatically
rules.impact: Missing audit records make tampering hard to prove and often go unnoticed until an incident review.

rules.title: The system shuts down when audit logs are full
rules.explanation: auditd can be configured to halt or enter single-user mode when the audit log filesystem has no free space, failing closed rather than continuing unaudited.
rules.impact: In high-security environments, continuing without space for audit records risks undetected unauthorized activity; availability is intentionally subordinated to audit integrity.

rules.title: The system warns when audit logs have insufficient space
rules.explanation: When the audit log is full the system must stop rather than drop records. Losing audit data silently defeats the purpose of auditing.
rules.impact: Timely warnings about insufficient space allow administrators to take action before the system stops recording audit events, which could result in the loss of critical security information.

Audit changes can be made only after a system reboot. Note: This setting will require a system reboot to update the active auditd configuration settings.
rules.impact: In immutable mode, unauthorized users cannot modify the audit system to potentially conceal malicious activity and then restore the audit rules. Users are likely to notice a system reboot, which can alert administrators to an attempt to make unauthorized audit changes.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/passwd are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/passwd lists local user accounts and must remain world-readable for normal system operation while writable only by root.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/passwd can create privileged accounts or alter user attributes used for access control.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/passwd- are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/passwd- is a backup of /etc/passwd and should have ownership and mode protections comparable to the primary file.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/group are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/group defines local groups and membership. It should be world-readable as required for normal operation and writable only by root.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/group can grant users membership in privileged groups without approved account-management processes.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/group- are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/group- is a backup of /etc/group and should be protected with ownership and mode settings comparable to the primary file.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shadow are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shadow stores local password hashes and related aging fields. It must not be readable by unprivileged users.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shadow- are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shadow- is a backup of /etc/shadow and contains the same sensitive password hash material as the primary file.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/gshadow are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/gshadow stores group passwords and administrator lists. Access should be limited to privileged accounts.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/gshadow- are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/gshadow- is a backup of /etc/gshadow and should receive protections equivalent to the primary file.
rules.impact: A user who can modify these files can add an account or change a password hash, which usually means full control of the host.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/shells are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/shells lists valid login shells consulted by some services when validating account shells.
rules.impact: Correct permissions on this file prevent unauthorized modification that could allow insecure shells to be added or secure shells to be removed.

rules.title: Permissions on /etc/security/opasswd are configured
rules.explanation: /etc/security/opasswd stores hashed previous passwords used by password-history mechanisms such as pam_pwhistory.
rules.impact: Protecting this file is critical, because its compromise could allow an attacker to obtain hashes of users' previous passwords.

rules.title: World-writable files and directories are protected
rules.explanation: World-writable filesystem objects can be modified by any local user. Sticky bits on shared directories or remediation of unexpected write bits limit abuse.
rules.impact: World-writable files and directories can be modified by any user on the system, which may lead to unauthorized changes, malware installation, or privilege escalation.

rules.title: No files or directories without an owner and group exist
rules.explanation: Ensure that no files or directories without an owner and group exist.
rules.impact: Orphaned files may result from improper user deletion or system errors and can pose a security risk because their access permissions may be incorrectly configured.

rules.title: SUID and SGID files are reviewed
rules.explanation: The file owner can set permissions to run the file with the owner's or group's permissions even if the user running the program is not the owner or a member of the group. The most common reason for using an SUID or SGID program is to allow users to perform functions (for example, changing a password) that require root privileges.
rules.impact: There are valid reasons for SUID and SGID programs, but it is important to identify and review such programs to ensure they are legitimate. Review the files returned by the action in the audit section and check whether system binaries have a checksum that differs from the package checksum. This indicates that the binary may have been replaced.

rules.title: Accounts in /etc/passwd use shadow passwords
rules.explanation: Local accounts should store an 'x' in the /etc/passwd password field and keep actual hashes in /etc/shadow.
rules.impact: Password hashes in world-readable /etc/passwd are immediately available for offline cracking; shadowing confines hashes to a restricted file.

rules.title: /etc/shadow password fields are not empty
rules.explanation: An empty password field in /etc/shadow lets the account log in without a password.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: All groups in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group
rules.explanation: A primary group referenced by a passwd entry but missing from /etc/group leaves the user with an undefined group, which breaks file access assumptions.
rules.impact: When the check fails the host deviates from the Ubuntu hardening baseline and the corresponding weakness remains exploitable until it is corrected.

rules.title: The shadow group is empty
rules.explanation: The shadow group allows system programs that require access to read /etc/shadow. Users should not be assigned to the shadow group.
rules.impact: All users assigned to the shadow group will be granted read access to /etc/shadow. If attackers can obtain read access to /etc/shadow, they can easily run a password-cracking program against the hashed passwords to crack them. Other security information stored in /etc/shadow (for example, expiration dates) may also be useful for compromising additional user accounts.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist
rules.explanation: Although the useradd program will not allow you to create a duplicate user identifier (UID), an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change the UID field.
rules.impact: Users must be assigned unique UIDs to ensure accountability and to provide appropriate access protection.

rules.title: No duplicate GIDs exist
rules.explanation: Although groupadd will not allow you to create a duplicate group identifier (GID), an administrator can manually edit /etc/group and change the GID field.
rules.impact: User groups should be assigned unique GIDs to ensure accountability and appropriate access protection.

rules.title: No duplicate user names exist
rules.explanation: Although the useradd program will not allow you to create a duplicate username, an administrator can manually edit /etc/passwd and change a username.
rules.impact: If a user is assigned a duplicate username, they will create files with the first UID for that username and access them in /etc/passwd. For example, if "test4" has UID 1000 and a subsequent "test4" entry has UID 2000, logging in as "test4" will use UID 1000. In effect, the UID is shared, which is a security issue.

rules.title: No duplicate group names exist
rules.explanation: Although groupadd will not allow you to create a duplicate group name, an administrator can manually edit /etc/group and change a group name.
rules.impact: If a group is assigned a duplicate group name, it will create files with the first GID for that group and gain access to them in /etc/group. Essentially, the GID is shared, which is a security issue.

rules.title: Local interactive user home directories are configured
rules.explanation: Home directories of interactive users exist, are owned by the user and are not readable by other users, so one account cannot inspect another.
rules.impact: Properly configured home directories protect user data from unauthorized access by other users and enforce the principle of least privilege.

rules.title: Access to local interactive user dot files is configured
rules.explanation: User startup and configuration files such as .bashrc, .profile, and SSH client settings should not be writable by other users.
rules.impact: Writable dotfiles allow injection of commands that execute when the user next logs in, enabling lateral movement under that user's privileges.
